newsitem.title: JAPAN: Leak, cover-up latest blow to Japan nuclear plans.
newsitem.headline: Leak, cover-up latest blow to Japan nuclear plans.

text.p: The shutdown of a nuclear plant in western Japan after a radiation leak this week has dealt yet another painful blow to the country's ambitious nuclear power programme, industry sources and analysts said on Wednesday.
The leak at the "Fugen" advanced thermal reactor on Monday was the third accident involving the state-run Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corp (PNC) in the past 16 months.
Authorities ordered the PNC to shut down the 165,000 kilowatt reactor from Tuesday night after learning it had waited 30 hours before reporting the leakage.

"The recent series of accidents has caused the public to become suspicious of Japan's nuclear power industry as a whole," said Kazuya Fujime, managing director of the Institute of Energy Economics (IEE).

Public opposition to nuclear power has already blocked the construction of new nuclear power plants, and power industry analysts said they expected the latest incident to further delay Japan's plans to boost dependency on nuclear power.
They said the nuclear development programme had already been seriously damaged by the revelations that the PNC had mishandled and attempted to cover-up the previous accidents.

"The accident at Fugen will fan public opposition towards nuclear power, making it even more difficult to promote nuclear power," said an analyst at Yamaichi Research Research Institute of Securities and Economics.
Japan relies on nuclear power for about a third of its power needs, a dependency it plans to boost to 42 percent by 2010.

Fujime cast doubt on this target. He said that at best the government would be able to expand nuclear capacity only to the extent necessary to maintain the nuclear industry's current share of total power supply.
Fugen, located in Fukui prefecture, runs on recycled plutonium as well as the enriched uranium used in conventional nuclear reactors, and is Japan's sole heavy-water reactor.

A PNC official said the radiation leak occurred when heavy water, containing the radioactive material tritium, leaked from a water purification system located in a separate building from the reactor. He said the size of the leakage was very small and had caused no injuries or damage to the environment.
One analyst, who asked not to be identified, said power utilities were in a way relieved that plans to construct nuclear power plants would be delayed.

"Power utilities are under heavy pressure from the government to bring electricity rates down," he said. "Running costs of nuclear power plants are low but other costs such as reprocessing used fuel, and scrapping old nuclear power plants are very high," he said.
In an economic reform programme launched last year, the government called on utilities to slash electricity rates to make them comparable to levels overseas.
Industry estimates show the average family in Japan pays about 20 percent more for its electricity than a German family and 30 percent more than a family in the United States.
However, delay or no delay, Japan's power utilities have little choice but to increase dependency on nuclear power, given growing energy demand, the IEE's Fujime said.
"Utilities will not be able to meet the country's electricity needs unless nuclear power plants are built."

An official of the government's Science and Technology Agency said permission to restart Fugen would be granted once the PNC had established proper internal reporting lines. He said the plant was not likely to remain shut more than a year.
"Given the situation the PNC is in, we are truly at a loss as to why the PNC cannot report accidents promptly to the authorities," the official said.

The PNC is already under fire for covering up its mishandling of Japan's worst nuclear accident -- a fire and explosion last month at a nuclear fuel reprocessing plant. It has admitted issuing a false report about safety procedures during the incident.

In 1995, PNC officials admitted they had lied about inspections and tried to suppress videotape footage of a massive coolant leak at the firm's Monju experimental fast-breeder reactor, not far from the site of Monday's leak.
